entries.note: The root box is right: Proto-Semitic *ʔabw- 'father' (Akk. abum, Ugar. ʾabu, Heb. ʾāḇ, Aram. ʾabbā, Arab. ʾab, Geʿez ʾab), an old nursery word, ultimately Proto-Afroasiatic; Klein s.v. Aboth says exactly this ('of uncertain origin, possibly traceable to *ab(a), a child's word for father'). Nourai's '2' is his homograph number (Ab 1 = water). Two branches of the chart are problematic and both hang on Arabic kunya-compounds in node #3: (a) the gibbon branch — Persian بوزینه is an inherited Iranian word (Wiktionary: inherited from Proto-Iranian, cf. Pashto bīzo; attested as būzīna, pl. būzīnagān already in the early NP Qurʾān commentary per Hübschmann, and lent onward to Old East Slavic obezĭjána and Old Turkic béčin) and French gibbon is of unknown origin, so the whole Arabic abū-zīnā > būzīne > bojīna > gibbon chain collapses; (b) the borage branch — Arabic abū ʿaraq 'father of sweat' as the source of Med.Lat. borrāgō is supported by Klein, AHD, Lokotsch no. 13 and Pihan, but rejected by Skeat, Webster and the OED/Etymonline in favour of Lat. borra/burra 'rough hair', so it is a live scholarly split, not a settled fact. Two printed-book errors (not extraction errors — checked against the page scan at 600 dpi): 'borrâco' in node #8 is a misprint for borrāgō, and 'Jaob' in node #16 for Joab. The JSON's «آبو» in node #2 IS an extraction artefact: the book prints أَبو (alef+hamza+fatha), read by OCR as alef-madda.

Cp. the first element in Abraham, Abner, Absalom, Abigail, and the second element in Joab, Moab, Barabbas… Cp. also borage.' This one page is the source of almost the whole chart.

nodes.derivation: Arabic أَبٌ ʾab-un 'father' continues Proto-Semitic *ʔabw- directly; the third radical wāw survives in the construct/nominative أَبُو ʾabū (acc. أَبَا ʾabā, gen. أَبِي ʾabī) — the 'six nouns' (al-asmāʾ al-sitta) declension — and in the plural آبَاء ʾābāʾ and the nisba أَبَوِيّ ʾabawī. Nourai's 'a.b.v' is his notation for the root ء ب و (ʾ-b-w), with v = wāw; that is exactly the root under which Wiktionary and the Arabic lexica file the word. ʾabū is the element that opens a kunya (Abū ʿAlī) and, by the same idiom, hundreds of Arabic plant- and animal-names ('father of X').

nodes.derivation: The derivation is right — Persian ابو abu is a straight Arabic loan, taken over with the kunya formula after the Islamic conquest and productive in Persian names from the 10th c. on: ابوعلی سینا, ابوالفضل, ابوالقاسم, ابوالحسن, ابوالفتح, with the colloquial contraction ابوال- > بوال- in بوالهوس bu'l-hawas 'capricious, given to whims' (Moʿin files this under بل 'مخفف ابوالقاسم و ابوالفضل و مانند آنها'). The nisba form ابوی abavī 'paternal' is used in Persian (but not in Arabic) as a polite word for 'my father'. What is wrong is the Persian script in the JSON: the printed page (checked at 600 dpi) has أَبو — alef with hamza and fatḥa — which the OCR turned into «آبو» with alef madda. آبو is a different Persian word entirely (Moʿin: آبو = نیلوفر آبی 'water lily'), so the JSON headword should read «ابو ( ابوی )».

nodes.derivation: Both words are Arabic kunya-compounds of ʾabū 'father of' (node #1). أبو عرق abū ʿaraq 'father of sweat' (root ع ر ق ʿ-r-q, cf. ʿaraq 'sweat, distilled juice' > arrack) is genuinely attested as the Arab physicians' name for borage, from its diaphoretic use, and is the etymon Klein, the AHD, Lokotsch (no. 13) and Pihan give for Med.Lat. borrāgō — that word is plausible (see node #8 for the dispute over whether Latin really took it). أبو زنا abū zinā 'father of fornication' (root ز ن ي, whence zinā 'illicit intercourse') as an Arabic name for the gibbon is the weak half: no Arabic lexicon consulted here lists it, and it is invoked only to explain Persian بوزینه, which is not an Arabic loan at all (node #4). Phonetically the derivation also fails: abū zinā would give Persian *abu-zenā, not būzīna with -īn-. Addi Shir, writing in Arabic, actually treats بوزینه as a foreign (Turkish/Persian) word for a monkey, not as Arabic.

nodes.derivation: The word and its meaning are right — NP بوزینه būzīna 'monkey, ape' (variants بوزینا, بوزنه, بوزنینه), quoted by Nourai from Rumi — but the Arabic parent is not. Modern Iranian etymology takes būzīna as inherited from Proto-Iranian, cognate with Pashto بيزو bīzo 'monkey'; Hübschmann already notes that it is the current NP replacement for the older Indic loan kabī/kapī (< Pahl. kapīk, Skt. kapi-) and that it is attested 'schon im alten Korancommentar' (the 10th-11th c. NP Tafsīr, pl. būzīnagān), i.e. before any large-scale Arabic influence on the vocabulary of fauna. Its own descendants run the other way: it was lent into Old East Slavic обезьꙗ́на obezĭjána (whence Russian обезьяна 'monkey') and probably into Old Turkic béčin. Formally, Arabic abū zinā could only have given *abuzenā; the -īna(g) of būzīna is an Iranian suffix. Moʿin, who tags every Arabic loan [ع.], gives بوزینه no origin tag at all.

nodes.derivation: No Hindustani (Urdu/Hindi) word bojīna 'ape' can be documented. The ordinary Hindustani words are bandar and, for the langur, lāṅgūr; the Indian gibbon (Hylobates hoolock) is called hūlak/hoolock, which is what Hobson-Jobson records as the Indian name Europeans actually met in Bengal and Assam ('HOOLOCK, s. Beng. hulak. The word is not in the Dicts.'). The OED's verdict on the supposed Indian source of gibbon is blunt — 'supposedly from a word in the French colonies of India but not found in any language there'. Nourai's bojīna looks like a link invented to bridge Persian būzīne (itself the wrong parent, node #4) to French gibbon; his only authority for it is Partridge, whose Origins is a popular etymological dictionary, not a source on Indic lexicon.

nodes.derivation: Empty pass-through node standing for French gibbon (18th c.). The chart's own NOTE — 'This monkey was taken to France from India in the 18th century' — is accurate and is Klein's: the animal and its name were brought to Europe by Joseph-François Dupleix (1697-1763), governor-general of the French possessions in India 1742-54, and the word first appears in French zoological writing (Buffon) in the 1760s. What is not supported is the arrow from Hindustani bojīna: the OED/Etymonline record the French word as of uncertain origin, 'supposedly from a word in the French colonies of India but not found in any language there', and the current Wiktionary proposal derives it, through folk etymology on the French surname Gibbon, from a Northern Aslian language of the Malay peninsula (cf. Batek kəboɲ) — i.e. from the gibbon's actual habitat rather than from India at all.

nodes.derivation: English gibbon is a straight borrowing of French gibbon, first recorded in English in 1770 as a name for the long-armed apes (Hylobates) that Dupleix's specimens had made known in Paris; no phonetic change beyond the English stress and /dʒ/. The link French > English is uncontroversial; only what stands behind French is unknown (node #6).

nodes.derivation: The Medieval Latin plant name is borrāgō, gen. borrāginis (whence It. borragine, borrana, Sp. borraja, Pg. borragem, Prov. borrage, Ger. Boretsch/Burrich). 'borrâco' is a misprint in Nourai's own printed page — I read the book scan at 600 dpi and it really does print 'borrâco', so this is the author's error, not the JSON extraction's. On the derivation itself scholarship is split. FOR the Arabic source: Klein ('ult. fr. Arab. abū ʿarak, lit. "father of sweat", so called by the Arab physicians because of its sudorific effect'), the AHD ('probably from Arabic bū ʿaraq, from ʾabū ʿaraq'), Lokotsch no. 13 ('hieraus lat. borrago… Trotz ML 1412 scheint diese Ableitung noch immer die beste'), and Pihan p. 76; the route is Arabic medical botany > Salernitan/Latin herbals of the 11th-13th c. > Romance. AGAINST: Skeat, Webster, and the OED (followed by Etymonline), which take borrāgō from Latin borra/burra 'rough hair, coarse wool' + -āgō (a common Latin plant-name suffix, cf. plantāgō, farrāgō), from the plant's famously bristly leaves — a formation that explains the -āgō suffix, which the Arabic etymology does not. Note that the Latin-borra account also weakens Klein's own cross-reference from arrack.

nodes.derivation: Med.Lat. borrāgō, acc. borrāginem, gave Old French borrache/borrace (13th c.), with the regular Gallo-Romance treatment of intervocalic -g- before a front vowel and the loss of the final syllable; the doublet with -rr- and the variant burage are both recorded. The modern French form is bourrache, with -ou- for the tonic o. Klein gives precisely 'OF. borrace (cp. its variant burage and F. bourrache)', so both of the chart's forms are documented — although Lokotsch assigns borrace to Italian rather than Old French, so the pair may conflate an Italian and a French form.

The English word's own history is not in doubt; only the ultimate source behind Medieval Latin is (node #8).

nodes.derivation: Biblical Hebrew אָב ʾāḇ 'father' (Nourai's 'abh' is the older transliteration with spirantised bēṯ, ʾāḇ) continues Proto-Semitic *ʾabw- with loss of the third radical in the free form; the wāw resurfaces in the construct plural אֲבוֹת ʾăḇōṯ and in ʾăḇī- in compound names. It is the exact cognate of Arabic ab (node #1) and Aramaic ʾabbā, not a borrowing from it — so the chart's two branches from the root box are correctly drawn as sisters.

nodes.derivation: English Abot / Aboth is the Hebrew plural אָבוֹת ʾăḇōṯ 'fathers' taken over unchanged as the title of the Mishnah tractate Pirqē ʾĀḇōṯ 'Chapters of the Fathers' (the Ethics of the Fathers) and, in the liturgy, of the first benediction of the ʿAmīdā. The construct plural preserves the original third radical (*ʾabaw-āt > ʾăḇōṯ), which is why the plural, not the singular, is the form English received. Nourai's spelling 'Abot' is Klein's own alternative spelling.

nodes.derivation: All six are genuine Hebrew names built on ʾāḇ 'father', five with ʾāḇ first and one (Joab) with it second, and Klein's p. 6-7 entries give Nourai's glosses almost word for word. אַבְנֵר ʾAḇnēr 'my father is light' = ʾăḇī + nēr 'lamp, light' (Klein compares the Babylonian PN Abunuri) — confirmed. אַבְשָׁלוֹם ʾAḇšālōm 'father is peace' = ʾāḇ + šālōm — confirmed. אֲבִיגַיִל ʾĂḇīgayil 'my father is rejoicing' = ʾăḇī + gīl 'to rejoice' — confirmed. אַבְרָם ʾAḇrām = ʾāḇ + rām 'high, exalted' (participle of rūm), so properly 'the father is exalted' rather than Nourai's 'high father' — a word-order quibble, not an error of substance. יוֹאָב Yōʾāḇ 'YHWH is (his) father', with Yō- the shortened theophoric of YHWH as in Joel, Jonathan, Joshua — confirmed. The one problem word is אַבְרָהָם ʾAḇrāhām: 'father of the multitude' is the explanation Genesis 17:5 itself supplies (ʾaḇ hămōn gōyim), and Klein follows it by positing *rāhām 'multitude' (comparing Arabic ruhām); modern scholarship generally treats that as a folk etymology attached to an already-old name and takes ʾAḇrāhām as a dialectal/expanded byform of ʾAḇrām ('the father is exalted'), the -h- being an Aramaic-style secondary expansion rather than a 'multitude' morpheme. Hence 'plausible' for the node as a whole.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaves 15-16 (printed pp. 6-7): 'Abner… Heb. Abhnēr, lit. "my father is light", fr. abh, "father", and nēr, "light"'; 'Absalom… Heb. Abhshālōm, lit. "father is peace"'; 'Abigail… Heb. Abhigáyil, lit. "my father is rejoicing"'; 'Abram… compounded of ābh, "father", and rām, "high, exalted"'; 'Abraham… Heb. Abhrāhām, lit. "father of the multitude", compounded of ābh, "father", and *rāhām, "multitude", which is rel. to Arab. ruhām, of s.m.; see Gen. 17:5'; 'Joab… fr. Heb. Yōʾāḇ, lit. "the Lord is (his) father"'. Every gloss on the chart is Klein's.

consulted.note: all six names, as quoted.

consulted.note: Genesis 17:4-5 glosses the name as ʾaḇ + hămōn 'father of many nations'; modern scholars (e.g. Thompson) read it as 'the father is exalted', the biblical gloss being a forgotten-etymology folk explanation, or as a dialectal variant of Abram.

nodes.derivation: The Arabic name is إِبْرَاهِيم Ibrāhīm (Nourai's 'Abrahim' is a loose transliteration; the Qurʾānic form has initial i- and -āhīm). It does go back to Hebrew ʾAḇrāhām, but not directly, and Nourai's single arrow flattens the step that Jeffery — the very reference he cites — spends the page arguing: a direct Hebrew borrowing would have produced *Abrāhām, and the Arabic vocalisation with -īm points to the Syriac/Christian-Aramaic ʾAḇrāhām as the immediate source, the same form that gave Geʿez ʾAbrəhām and Armenian Abraham. Wiktionary likewise files إبراهيم as 'borrowed from Aramaic אַבְרָהָם', with Biblical Hebrew behind that. The word entered Arabic in the pre-Islamic Christian/Jewish milieu of the Ḥijāz and is Qurʾānic (some 69 occurrences), and the Muslim philologists themselves (as-Suyūṭī, al-Jawālīqī) already classed it as a foreign word.

ref_check.note: FVQ_pages.txt leaves 62-63 (printed pp. 44-45): the entry إبراهيم begins on p. 44 and continues 'ultimately derived from Heb. אברהם. If the name had come direct from the Heb. we should have expected the form *Abrāhām… we learn from as-Suyūṭī, Muzhir, i, 138, and al-Jawālīqī, 8, that some early authorities recognized it as a foreign borrowing… The common Syr. form is ʾAḇrāhām which is obviously the source of both the Eth. and the Arm.' So Jeffery supports the Hebrew ultimate origin but explicitly denies the direct Hebrew > Arabic route Nourai's arrow draws.

consulted.note: as quoted — Hebrew ultimately, Syriac/Aramaic immediately.
Klein treats only the Hebrew and the European forms; he does not mention the Arabic name.

nodes.derivation: Persian ابراهیم is the Arabic Qurʾānic name taken over unchanged in spelling after the conquest and read in Persian phonology as Ebrāhīm (Classical Persian Ibrāhīm), Arabic i- being realised as e- in New Persian; Wiktionary lists Classical Persian ابراهیم explicitly as a descendant of Arabic إبراهيم. It is a common Persian given name from the earliest Islamic-Persian literature on, and Nourai's Rumi couplet (بت شکستی گیرم ابراهیم‌وار / کو بت تن را فدا کردن به نار) is the standard literary allusion to Abraham the idol-breaker thrown into Nimrod's fire.

ref_check.note: Nourai gives this node no reference of his own; nothing to check.

consulted.note: the Adena 2-vol abridgement of Farhang-e Fārsi covers the lexicon only; ابراهیم appears solely in running definitions (مقام ابراهیم, ملت ابراهیم), since proper names are in vols 5-6 (Aʿlām) of the 6-vol edition, which is not digitised.
ابراهیم occurs 27 times but only in Moʿin's introduction and in citations (e.g. 'ابو ابراهیم فارابی'); Borhān-e Qāṭeʿ has no headword for the personal name.

nodes.words: Abraham, Abram, Abner, Absalom, Abigail, Jaob
nodes.derivation: All six English names reached English from Hebrew through the Greek of the Septuagint/New Testament and Late Latin of the Vulgate (Gk. Ἀβραάμ, Ἀβεννήρ, Ἀβεσσαλώμ, Ἀβιγαία, Ἰωάβ > Late L. Ābrahām, Abner, Absalom, Abigail, Joab), and were spread as given names by the Bible and, from the 16th c., by Puritan naming practice; Abigail additionally became a common noun 'lady's maid' after 1 Sam. 25:25, where she calls herself a handmaid. 'Jaob' is a misprint for Joab in the printed book itself (verified on the 600 dpi page scan), not an extraction error; the same name is spelled correctly as 'Joab' in the parent node #13.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaves 15-16 and leaf ~430 carry all six as English headwords with Hebrew etymologies: 'Abraham, masc. PN.; in the Bible, the first of the patriarchs…', 'Abram…', 'Abner, n., masc. PN.…', 'Absalom…', 'Abigail, fem. PN.…', 'Joab, 1) masc. PN.; 2) in the Bible, the chief captain of David's army. — Late L. Joab, fr. Gk. Ἰωάβ, fr. Heb. Yōʾāḇ'. Klein's Joab entry also supplies the Greek/Late Latin route this node needs.
Nourai gives no page; the 1975/76 New College Edition is lending-only, and biographical/biblical entries are not in the Watkins IE-roots appendix that is available locally (AHD_watkins1985.txt).

consulted.note: as quoted; 'Late L. Joab, fr. Gk. Ἰωάβ, fr. Heb. Yōʾāḇ' gives the transmission route.
